ECE 6390

Finding the packet and keeping the symbol clock

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows a known 13-chip header located by its correlation peak, and the timing error that a small symbol-clock mismatch accumulates across a packet.

A receiver must find where a packet begins before any matched-filter sample means anything. A known header or preamble p[k] of N_h samples supplies the reference. For received complex-baseband samples r[k], the trial offset q gives C[q] = (1/N_h) Σ r[k + q] p*[k]. Its magnitude peaks where the stored header lines up with the received copy; each offset step is one sample interval.

A good header has a sharp autocorrelation. The 13-chip Barker sequence used here sums to 13 when aligned, and its aperiodic sidelobes have magnitude at most 1, so noise must be large before a wrong offset wins. Practical receivers also estimate carrier offset from the header and interpolate between samples to refine the start time.

After estimating a start time t̂₀ and symbol interval T̂, the receiver makes decision n at t̂ₙ = t̂₀ + nT̂, with timing error eₙ = (t̂₀ − t₀) + n(T̂ − T). A start error shifts every decision equally; an interval mismatch grows linearly along the packet. Clock tracking updates T̂ so the drift never uses up the eye’s timing margin.

Example

With T = 1 µs and a 10-parts-per-million interval error, T̂ − T = 10 ps. After 1000 symbols the accumulated error is 10 ns, or 0.01T. Reaching 0.1T without tracking would take 10,000 symbols.

Practice

1. A receiver’s symbol interval is 50 ppm long. Without tracking, after how many symbols does its decision time slip by a quarter symbol?

Solve n × 50 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.25.

n = 0.25/(50 × 10⁻⁶) = 5000 symbols. A longer packet needs timing updates before then.

2. Why does a header with low autocorrelation sidelobes help in noise?

Compare the score at the correct offset with the scores at wrong offsets.

Wrong offsets score near zero while the aligned offset collects the full header, so noise must add a large error before a wrong offset exceeds the true peak. High sidelobes would let smaller noise produce a false start.
